items.excerpt: We are piloting a new show on Latent Space: High Taste Testers, a variant of our food show where we pull you in to a typical lunch conversation in San Francisco. All your favorite talking points, starting with Dev Day and going into the latest models and assistants, are here:Let us know your feedback!AI News for 10/15/2026-10/16/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapUS Open-Weights Push: Muse Spark Open and Reflection BeamMuse Spark Open (Meta): An 816B-total, 42B-active MoE with open weights. Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 (AA).Architecture and footprint: 62 layers, GQA with 16 KV heads, 8 of 256 experts active per token, a 1.8B Perception Encoder and 1M context. Inputs are text, image, video and audio; output is text. BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. Meta’s NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts, cutting weights to about 530GB. Meta says that fits on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, 8 H200s or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios.Pricing and efficiency: Together, Fireworks and Baseten charge $1.25/$4.25 per M input/output tokens, with $0.15 cached input. AA puts the cost at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It uses 40k output tokens per task, the fewest among the top nine open models (cost). Vals counts 55.5M output tokens across its index, the fewest of any open model, but says input tokens drive most of its cost (Vals).Weak spot: It ranks last among the top nine open models on AA’s four agentic evals while leading open models on AA-Omniscience. Vals places it #12 among open-weight models and #38 overall (Vals). Arena ranks it the top US open model on Code Arena WebDev with 1511 points, #13 among open models (Arena)

items.title: High Taste Testers: OpenAI Shipped Everything. What Actually Works?
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: Six AI power users compare what actually works—and what falls apart once you start using it. Ben Davis, Ben Hylak, Dex Horthy, Allison Durham, Alex Volkov, and swyx discuss OpenAI DevDay, coding agents, personal assistants, model preferences, and the gap between impressive AI capabilities and useful products. From Pi-powered personal agents and decision models to subagents, context management, prompt injection, and assistants that can spend money: what deserves a place in your daily workflow?
